subtype_info: frontal lobe and multiple intracranial tuberculomas
title: Frontal lobe tuberculoma
case_text:
A 4-year-old girl presented with a history of multiple episodes of seizures since the last one and half years. The seizures were varying in semiology:initially multifocal with secondary generalization and later tonic seizures with frequency gradually increasing from once every 6 months to once every 2 weeks. There was no fever, vomiting or headache. On examination, she had papilloedema and brisk deep tendon reflexes. Weight was 13 kg (<15th centile) and blood pressure 110/70. Other systems were normal. There was no focal neurological deficit.
On investigation, haemogram, chest X-ray was normal. Computed tomography (CT) scan brain showed evidence of a large conglomerate ring enhancing focal lesion in the parafalcine frontal cortices mainly on the left side with extensive white matter hypodensity in both frontal lobes (Fig. 1). Small tuberculomas were also seen in the left occipital lobe and left lateral inferior cerebellum, tegmentum of pons and right temporal lobe. 
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain showed a 5.7 x 3.9 x 4.8 cm-sized heterogeneously hyperintense peripherally enhancing conglomerate lesion involving the left frontal parafalcine region crossing onto the midline and right parafalcine frontal lobe, extending into the genu of the corpus callosum and showing patchy restricted diffusion. The lesion showed extensive perilesional vasogenic oedema (Fig. 2) with multiple ring and disc enhancing lesions seen in the bilateral cerebral and cerebellar parenchyma and in the right hemipons. Magnetic resonance spectroscopy revealed lactate double peak and diffuse reduction in all the metabolite peaks suggestive of tuberculoma. The Mantoux test was negative. 
Patient was started on i.v. dexamethasone, which was given for 5 days, and subsequently lumbar puncture was done. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination was normal. CSF Gene Xpert revealed no Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, and TB MGIT was negative for Acid Fast Bacilli. Antitubercular treatment (ATT) with isoniazid (10 mg/kg/day), rifampicin (10 mg/kg/day), ethambutol (20 mg/kg/day) and pyrazinamide (35 mg/kg/day) along with oral prednisolone at 2 mg/kg/day was started on Day 5 of hospitalization. The child improved, seizures stopped and the papilloedema gradually disappeared.
A neurosurgical opinion for biopsy of lesion was taken, but in view of classical MRI findings, it was deferred.
Follow-up MRI brain after 8 months of treatment showed a mild reduction in the size of the lesion to 4 x 4 x 2.3 cm with mild perilesional vasogenic oedema. The ring enhancing lesions in the bilateral cerebral hemispheres were still present. However, the cerebellar and pontine lesions had disappeared (Fig. 3). Child is on regular follow-up.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: frontal lobe and multiple intracranial tuberculomas
